data.title: Split-screen
data.tagline: Give two parallel tasks two near-equal halves of one view
data.description: Login pages often put the brand story on the left half and the form on the right; entry pages can give personal and enterprise plans one half each. It only counts as split-screen when both sides truly run parallel tasks; on phones a side-by-side split is unreadable, so stack the areas and decide yourself which one comes first.

distinctions.label: Sidebar Layout
distinctions.explanation: In Sidebar the sidebar is navigation with clearly less weight than the workspace; in Split-screen both sides carry near-equal, independent tasks.

distinctions.label: Image plus text
distinctions.explanation: In an image-plus-text row the image only serves the text; in Split-screen each side carries its own task or entry, and removing either one loses a real job.

use: Login and signup pages: brand story on one side, the form on the other
Two audience entries: personal vs business, buyer vs seller
Two product paths: start a trial vs book a demo
Two plans or versions compared side by side at similar weight
avoid: One side is only a decorative image while the other holds the only task
A wide content area with a narrow sidebar is a sidebar layout instead
Keeping the side-by-side split on phones until text and buttons shrink
Cramming both halves full until the first screen becomes two crowded pages

lessonPractice.title: A product login page puts a brand story on the left half and the login form on the right. The delivered mobile version keeps the side-by-side layout, squeezing text and buttons. What should you do?

options.label: Stack the two areas on mobile with the login form first, then verify inputs and buttons stay usable
options.feedback: Stacking restores readable width; the form is the task visitors came to complete, so it leads.

options.label: Keep the two columns and scale both areas down proportionally to fit the phone
options.feedback: Proportional shrinking crushes inputs and buttons; mobile needs rearrangement, not a scaled-down desktop layout.

options.label: Remove the brand area on phones and keep only the login form
options.feedback: The brand area builds trust for first-time visitors; try restacking first and remove it only when it is proven dispensable.

data.agentPrompt: Make the login page a split-screen: the left half carries the brand intro with a “Learn more” entry, the right half carries the login form; both sides are parallel tasks with similar visual weight. On phones, stack them vertically with the form first. Then check on desktop and mobile: does each side read as its own task, and are inputs and buttons usable on the phone.
